source_refs.note: Book p. 227-228: 12.2.7 proof, Deduction lim (e^x - 1)/x = 1, Important Result to Remember (i)-(ii), Example 7 (i)-(ii)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
This result is the key to every limit of the form \(\frac{a^{x}-1}{x}\). Notice that putting \(x = 0\) gives \(\frac{a^{0}-1}{0} = \frac{0}{0}\), which has no meaning, so the limit has to be found by a trick. The trick is to change the variable so that the limit of 12.2.6, \(\lim_{y \to 0}(1+y)^{\frac{1}{y}} = e\), appears.
Here \(a > 0\) and \(a \ne 1\) (so that \(\log_{a}\) makes sense).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why does \(y \to 0\)? As \(x \to 0\), \(a^{x} \to a^{0} = 1\), so \(y = a^{x} - 1 \to 0\). The third line uses the definition of a logarithm: \(a^{x} = N\) means \(x = \log_{a} N\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
The book prints the last value as \(\log_{e}^{a}\) (the \(a\) raised like a power), and writes \(\log_{e}^{e}\) in the same way in the Deduction below. The correct notation is the logarithm of \(a\) to base \(e\):
\[= \dfrac{1}{\log_{a} e} = \log_{e} a\]
\[\lim_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{e^{x}-1}{x}\right) = \log_{e} e = 1\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Two small steps are hidden here.
1. \(\frac{1}{y}\log_{a}(1+y) = \log_{a}(1+y)^{\frac{1}{y}}\), by the log law \(k\log N = \log N^{k}\).
2. \(\frac{1}{\log_{a} e} = \log_{e} a\), by the change of base rule \(\log_{a} e = \frac{\log_{e} e}{\log_{e} a} = \frac{1}{\log_{e} a}\).

blocks.text_alt: the limit as x tends to 0 of (a to the power x minus 1) over x equals log of a to the base e

blocks.text:
We know that
\[\lim_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{a^{x}-1}{x}\right) = \log_{e} a \quad \text{...(i)}\]
Put \(a = e\) in (i), we know
\[\lim_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{e^{x}-1}{x}\right) = \log_{e}^{e} = 1\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
As above, the book prints \(\log_{e}^{e}\); it should read
\[\lim_{x \to 0}\left(\dfrac{e^{x}-1}{x}\right) = \log_{e} e = 1\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why? \(e > 1\), so its powers grow without bound: \(e^{10} \approx 22026\). For negative powers, \(e^{-x} = \frac{1}{e^{x}}\) is 1 divided by a huge number, so it gets close to 0. The graph of \(y = e^{x}\) rises steeply to the right and flattens towards the \(x\)-axis to the left.

blocks.title: Example 7
blocks.problem:
Express each limit in terms of \(e\).
(i) \(\lim_{n \to +\infty}\left(1+\frac{3}{n}\right)^{2n}\)
(ii) \(\lim_{n \to 0}(1+2n)^{\frac{1}{n}}\)
steps:
Given: (i) \(\left(1+\frac{3}{n}\right)^{2n}\) with \(n \to +\infty\); (ii) \((1+2n)^{\frac{1}{n}}\) with \(n \to 0\).
To find: each limit as a power of \(e\).
Method: both have the shape "1 + small quantity" raised to a large power. Rewrite each one so that it contains exactly \(\left(1+\frac{1}{m}\right)^{m}\) (for \(m \to \infty\)) or \((1+m)^{\frac{1}{m}}\) (for \(m \to 0\)), whose limit is \(e\).

Part (i), Step 1: Compare with the standard limit
Observe the resemblance of the limit with \(\lim_{n \to \infty}\left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right)^{n} = e\).
Why: the standard form has 1 over the variable inside and the same variable as the power. Here we have \(\frac{3}{n}\) inside and \(2n\) as the power, so we must adjust both.

Part (i), Step 2: Make the inside match
\[\dfrac{3}{n} = \dfrac{1}{\;n/3\;}\]
Why: we want 1 over something; \(\frac{3}{n}\) is the same as 1 divided by \(\frac{n}{3}\). So the "something" is \(\frac{n}{3}\), and the power should be \(\frac{n}{3}\) too.

Part (i), Step 3: Make the power match
\[\left(1+\dfrac{3}{n}\right)^{2n} = \left[\left(1+\dfrac{3}{n}\right)^{\frac{n}{3}}\right]^{6}\]
\[= \left[\left(1+\dfrac{1}{\frac{n}{3}}\right)^{\frac{n}{3}}\right]^{6}\]
Why: by the law \((a^{p})^{q} = a^{pq}\), \(\frac{n}{3} \times 6 = 2n\), so nothing has changed; we have only split the power into \(\frac{n}{3}\) (the matching part) and 6 (the extra part).

Part (i), Step 4: Take the limit
Put \(m = \frac{n}{3}\). When \(n \to +\infty\), \(m \to +\infty\).
\[\lim_{n \to +\infty}\left(1+\dfrac{3}{n}\right)^{2n} = \lim_{m \to +\infty}\left[\left(1+\dfrac{1}{m}\right)^{m}\right]^{6}\]
\[= e^{6}\]
Why: the bracket tends to \(e\) (12.2.6), and the limit of a power is the power of the limit (Theorem on limits), so the answer is \(e^{6}\).

Part (ii), Step 1: Compare with the standard limit
Observe the resemblance of the limit with \(\lim_{x \to 0}(1+x)^{\frac{1}{x}} = e\) (the Deduction in 12.2.6).
Why: here the variable goes to 0, so we use the zero form. Inside we have \(2n\), so the power should be \(\frac{1}{2n}\), but we have \(\frac{1}{n}\).

Part (ii), Step 2: Make the power match
\[\lim_{n \to 0}(1+2n)^{\frac{1}{n}} = \lim_{n \to 0}\left[(1+2n)^{\frac{1}{2n}}\right]^{2}\]
Why: \(\frac{1}{2n} \times 2 = \frac{1}{n}\), so the expression is unchanged.

Part (ii), Step 3: Substitute and take the limit
Put \(m = 2n\); when \(n \to 0\), \(m \to 0\).
\[\lim_{n \to 0}(1+2n)^{\frac{1}{n}} = \lim_{m \to 0}\left[(1+m)^{\frac{1}{m}}\right]^{2}\]
\[= e^{2}\]
Why: \((1+m)^{\frac{1}{m}} \to e\) as \(m \to 0\), so its square tends to \(e^{2}\).

Check:
For (i), a large value \(n = 3000\) gives \((1.001)^{6000} \approx 402.2\), and \(e^{6} \approx 403.4\).
For (ii), a small value \(n = 0.001\) gives \((1.002)^{1000} \approx 7.374\), and \(e^{2} \approx 7.389\). The values agree more closely as \(n\) gets nearer its limit.

blocks.text:
In the book, part (ii) begins: "Observe the resemblance of the limit with
\[\lim_{n \to 0}(1+2n)^{\frac{1}{n}} = e\]"
and its last line reads
\[= \lim_{m \to 0}\left[(1+m)^{m}\right]^{2} = e^{2}\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
1. The book says to compare with \(\lim_{n \to 0}(1+2n)^{\frac{1}{n}} = e\). That statement is false (this limit is \(e^{2}\), the answer of the example). The standard limit to compare with is
\[\lim_{m \to 0}(1+m)^{\frac{1}{m}} = e\]
2. In the last line the book prints the power of \((1+m)\) as \(m\); it must be \(\frac{1}{m}\):
\[\lim_{m \to 0}\left[(1+m)^{\frac{1}{m}}\right]^{2} = e^{2}\]
The final answer \(e^{2}\) is correct.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{a^{x}-1}{x} = \log_{e} a\) for \(a > 0\), \(a \ne 1\).
2. Special case \(a = e\): \(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{e^{x}-1}{x} = 1\).
3. \(e^{x} \to \infty\) as \(x \to \infty\) and \(e^{x} \to 0\) as \(x \to -\infty\).
4. For limits like \(\left(1+\frac{k}{n}\right)^{pn}\): split the power so that the standard form \(\left(1+\frac{1}{m}\right)^{m}\) appears; the answer is \(e^{kp}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(\lim_{x \to 0}\frac{a^{x}-1}{x} = \log_{a} e\). The base and the number are the other way round: the answer is \(\log_{e} a\).
2. Changing the power without balancing it: \(\left(1+\frac{3}{n}\right)^{2n}\) is \(\left[\left(1+\frac{3}{n}\right)^{\frac{n}{3}}\right]^{6}\), not \(\left[\left(1+\frac{3}{n}\right)^{\frac{n}{3}}\right]^{2}\). Always check that the two powers multiply back to the original power.
3. Forgetting to change the limit when changing the variable (\(n \to \infty\) becomes \(m \to \infty\); \(n \to 0\) becomes \(m \to 0\)).
